title: Huntington First Purchase (1653)
summary: A 1653 agreement brought a broad part of Matinecock homeland under an English land claim, from Cold Spring Harbor toward Northport Harbor. Its boundary language and conditions matter as much as the word “purchase.”
address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
map_geometry_source: Approximate historical area; cited boundary evidence and modern shoreline method in Location section. Reviewed September 26, 2026.
why_this_matters: A colonial land record describes a claim made at a particular time. Read its conditions and the people affected alongside the map; an outlined claim is not proof that Native relationships or rights ended.
introduction_title: Land, records and continuing Native history
introduction_content: A 1653 agreement brought a broad part of Matinecock homeland under an English land claim, from Cold Spring Harbor toward Northport Harbor. Its boundary language and conditions matter as much as the word “purchase.”
history_content:
Raseokan and other Native signatories entered an agreement with Richard Holbrook, Robert Williams and Daniel Whitehead. The surviving transcription names Nachaquatacke and Opeatkontycke, the northern sea and the southern extent of Raseokan’s bounds. It required the bounds to be shown within twenty days and provided that the writing would be void if they did not meet the stated expectation. Those conditions show why a deed must be read rather than treated as a simple disappearance of Native land or people.

Town of Huntington Archives, The First Purchase (April 2, 1653), deed transcription by Town Archivist Antonia S. Mattheou, p. 1. William H. Frohlich, Huntington’s Quirky History, Huntington Historical Society, March 31, 2020; illustrated 2003 Huntington purchases map, red First Purchase area.
whereintheworld_content:
This is an approximate interpretation of the Town Archives’ Cold Spring Harbor–Northport Harbor–Long Island Sound–Old Country Road description, checked against the Historical Society’s purchase map. Modern shorelines orient the coastal edges. The inland connecting lines broadly follow the described corridor; they do not recover every seventeenth-century boundary mark. Separate Lloyd Neck and Eaton’s Neck claims are not represented as part of this transaction.
